Learning Objectives
Identify appropriate imaging studies for the evaluation and acute management of pelvic ring
fractures.
Outline indications for and the timing of circumferential pelvic compression.
Determine anatomic considerations for the classification and management of pelvic ring
fractures.
Assess the importance of multidisciplinary management via hospital-based protocols.
Determine indications for urgent and emergent surgical stabilization of pelvic ring fractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

The pelvic ring consists of two innominate bones (left and right), each of which consists of the
pubis, ilium, and ischium (Figure 1). Each hemipelvis is attached to the other anteriorly via the
symphysis and posteriorly to the axial skeleton via the sacrum. Multiple ligamentous
structures secure the pelvic bones to maintain alignment and stability.
The major neurovascular structures supplying the lower extremities are intimately associated
with and supported by the pelvic ligaments (Figure 2). Injuries to the pelvic bones and
ligaments may injure these neurovascular structures. Bleeding of the arterial and venous
plexus within the true pelvis is associated with severe pelvic ring disruptions, leading to shock,
and may be fatal.
Pelvic ring disruption is an independent risk predictor for death following acute injury.1,2

bony anatomy of the pelvic ring. (Courtesy of Joshua L. Gary, MD, Los Angeles, CA.)

Overview
Pelvic ring disruptions encompass a broad spectrum of injury severity and morbidities.
Pelvic ring disruptions (high- and low-energy mechanisms of injury) may result in neurologic
deficits and posttraumatic deformity, which may lead to long-term pain, functional deficits,
and permanent disability.

Overview
Pelvic ring disruptions affect adult and pediatric patients. They should be evaluated and
managed in the same manner regardless of patient age. The pelvis represents the
junction between the spine and the lower extremities. The complex vascular and
neurologic anatomy with associated visceral structures of the abdomen creates potential

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001082
3/35

for complex injuries to multiple systems requiring the expertise of various medical
subspecialties.
Epidemiology
The incidence of pelvic ring disruption varies with geographic and societal factors but is
estimated to occur in approximately 20 per 100,000 individuals.
A bimodal age distribution exists, with older patients sustaining injuries from low-energy,
ground-level falls and younger patients sustaining injuries from high-energy mechanisms of
injury.
As many as 25% of polytrauma patients have an associated pelvic ring disruption.

Epidemiology
Pelvic ring disruptions represent approximately 3% of all fractures. A prospective study
from New South Wales, Australia demonstrated an incidence of 23 per 100,000 persons
with injuries almost evenly divided between low-energy mechanisms of injuries in older
patients and higher energy mechanisms of injury in younger patients.3 As many as 25%
of patients who sustain blunt polytrauma (Injury Severity Score =16) have a pelvic ring
disruption.4 Evaluation of patients who sustain blunt trauma according to Advanced
Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol begins with an AP view of the pelvis shortly after
arrival in the emergency department to identify injuries and initiate management
without delay. A thorough physical examination and diagnostic imaging studies should
be performed to identify all injuries throughout the body. Overall mortality from pelvic
fracture is 9%; however, the mortality rate in patients who arrive at the emergency
department in shock with a pelvic ring disruption from blunt trauma (systolic blood
pressure <90 mm Hg) is higher than 30%.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The innominate bones (pubis, ilia, ischia) and the sacrum are joined by the symphysis pubis,
sacrospinous, sacrotuberous, and anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments to form the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic Ring Fractures: Evaluation and Acute Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001082
4/35

pelvic ring.
The posterior sacroiliac ligaments are the strongest ligaments in the human body. In contrast
to the anterior sacroiliac ligaments, which are a tension band spanning the sacroiliac joint, the
posterior sacroiliac ligaments are intra-articular, and help resist and maintain vertical stability
of each hemipelvis.
The pelvic floor musculature (in concert with the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments) is
an important secondary stabilizer of the pelvic ring, and contains many of the major
neurovascular structures that traverse the pelvis from the trunk to the lower extremities.
Variations in sacral anatomy are common with sacral dysmorphism, characterized by altered
osseous anatomy and neural tunnels in the upper sacral segment (Figure 3).
Figure 3 AP three-dimensional, surface-rendered CT reconstruction image of a pelvis shows
sacral dysmorphism, with an upsloping sacral ala, mammillary bodies, and sacralization of a
lower lumbar segment. (Courtesy of Joshua L. Gary, MD, Los Angeles, CA.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Each hemipelvis is formed by the fusion of the pubis, ilium, and ischium through skeletal
maturation into adulthood. Anteriorly, the hemipelves are connected by the cartilage of
the symphyseal disk and ligaments. Each hemipelvis connects to the axial skeleton
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic Ring Fractures: Evaluation and Acute Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001082
5/35

through the sacroiliac joint via anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments that provide
rotational, translational, and axial stability. Sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments
connect the sacrum to the ischial spine and the ischial tuberosity, respectively (Figure 4).
Figure 4 AP three-dimensional, surface-rendered CT reconstruction image of a pelvis
shows the ligamentous anatomy. (Courtesy of Joshua L. Gary, MD, Los Angeles, CA.)
Sequential disruption of the ligamentous structures and the pelvic floor progressively
decreases the stability of the pelvic ring. In general, disruption of the pubic symphysis
and the anterior sacroiliac ligaments (plus or minus the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous
ligaments) leads to external rotational instability of the hemipelvis without loss of axial
stability. After additional disruption of the pelvic floor and attenuation of the posterior
sacroiliac ligaments, flexion/extension instability may result, culminating in complete
axial instability of the hemipelvis if the posterior sacroiliac ligaments are completely
disrupted.
Variations in sacral anatomy (sacral dysmorphism) arise from the spectrum of
segmentation anomalies of the axial skeleton at the level of the lumbosacral spine.
Evidence of this is found in approximately 30% to 40% of patients with pelvic fracture
and is characterized by the following criteria: an upsloping sacral ala, mamillary bodies, a
residual disk between the upper and second sacral segments, undulating sacroiliac
joints, and noncircular neural foramina.6 A thorough understanding of these osteologic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic Ring Fractures: Evaluation and Acute Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001082
6/35

variations and their anatomic implications is critical for safe placement of implants in the
posterior pelvic ring.7
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
90% of patients with a pelvic fracture admitted to a level I trauma center are injured in a motor
vehicle or motorcycle collision, automobile versus pedestrian injury, or a fall.
Mechanisms of injury that cause internal rotation of a hemipelvis decrease the volume of the
pelvic ring, and mechanisms of injury that cause external rotation of a hemipelvis increase the
volume of the pelvic ring.
Because of ring mechanics, patients with normal bone quality will almost always have an
anterior pelvic ring injury (pubic symphysis dislocation and/or ramus fracture) associated with
a posterior pelvic ring injury (sacral/iliac fracture and/or sacroiliac joint dislocation).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Fractures in patients with osteopenia may result from low-energy, ground-level falls,
whereas high-energy mechanisms of injury, such as motor vehicle and motorcycle
collisions and falls from height, are required to disrupt the pelvic ring in patients without
osteopenia. In a prospective study of patients admitted to several level I trauma centers
over 2 years, 37% of injuries resulted from motor vehicle collisions, 26% of injuries
resulted from falls, 16% of injuries resulted from automobile versus pedestrian injuries,
and 11% of injuries resulted from motorcycle collisions.5 In general, internal rotation of a
hemipelvis decreases the volume of a pelvic ring and generally does not correlate with
large amounts of internal hemorrhage because the intrapelvic vasculature does not
experience tensile forces that cause disruption. External rotation of a hemipelvis
exposes neurovascular structures to tension and shear, leading to potential disruption
and associated bleeding and traumatic neurologic injury.
Risk Factors

9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic Ring Fractures: Evaluation and Acute Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001082
7/35

Osteopenia and osteoporosis are risk factors for pelvic ring disruption in patients who sustain
a low-energy fall.
Behaviors such as alcohol and illicit substance use place patients at higher risk for vehicular
collisions and other high-energy blunt-trauma injuries. Approximately two-thirds of trauma
patients test positive for alcohol and/or illicit drugs.8

Risk Factors
Similar to many musculoskeletal injuries, pelvic ring disruptions have a bimodal age
distribution, with older patients more likely to be involved in lower energy mechanisms
of injury and have osteopenia and younger patients more likely to be involved in high-
energy trauma.
In Germany, the incidence of osteoporotic pelvic ring fractures in patients older than 60
years is 224 per 100,000 individuals per year and continues to rise as the population
ages. One-year mortality rates as high as 27% have been reported.9 Preventive therapies
with calcium, magnesium, and vitamin D in combination with regular screening via bone
mineral density studies and subsequent medical management of osteopenia and
osteoporosis help mitigate morbidity and mortality.
Associated Injuries
Patients who sustain high-energy trauma must be systematically evaluated from head to toe to
identify and appropriately manage all injuries.
Genitourinary trauma is commonly associated with pelvic ring disruption; this includes bladder
rupture (Figure 5), urethral disruption, erectile dysfunction in males, vaginal laceration in
females, and various other injuries to male and female genitalia.

pelvic ring disruption. (Courtesy of Joshua L. Gary, MD, Los Angeles, CA.)
Disruption of the vascular structures of the pelvis leads to bleeding and hemorrhage, with the
potential for death from exsanguination, hypotension, and shock.
Neurologic injury may result from traction injuries associated with sacroiliac dislocations or
crush injuries associated with sacral fractures that disrupt the sacral foramina or spinal canal.
(Figure 6)

Associated Injuries
A National Trauma Data Bank study showed that 5% of patients with a pelvic ring
disruption had an associated genitourinary injury, with men more commonly injured
than women. In addition to genitourinary injury, men had longer hospital and intensive
care unit length of stays and increased mortality, indicating they had more severe
injuies.10 Intrapelvic hemorrhage and its association with increased morbidity and
mortality is correlated with increasingly severe injuries to the pelvic ring. Hemodynamic
shock on arrival to the hospital (systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg) has been found to
be an independent risk factor for increased in-hospital mortality in multiple studies.1,2
Mortality rates higher than 30% are reported in patients who sustain blunt trauma, have
a pelvic ring disruption, and arrive at the emergency department in shock.5 Recent
studies have demonstrated much lower rates of neurologic injuries in patients with a
sacral fracture (4% versus 22%) versus historical rates previously published.11 Neurologic
injury has been associated with poorer long-term outcomes after pelvic ring disruption
in some studies;12 however, other studies have shown no association between
neurologic injury and poorer long-term outcomes.13
Injury Classification
The three classification systems most commonly used to describe pelvic fracture are the
Young-Burgess, Tile/Pennal, and OTA/AO Foundation classification systems. (Figure 7)

Issues with interobserver and intra-observer reliability exist with each of these classification
systems, and associated acetabular injuries may further complicate accurate classification.
Low-energy pelvic fractures in pathologic or osteopenic bone often do not conform to the
commonly used classification systems.
Traumatic lumbopelvic dissociation (disruption of the connection of the pelvis and lower
extremities from the axial skeleton) may or may not be associated with disruption of the pelvic
ring. It was initially described by Roy-Camille, and is classified into U, H, and Y patterns (Figure
8).

Injury Classification
The Tile/Pennal classification system describes pelvic ring disruptions based on the
rotational (partial injury) and vertical (complete injury) stability of the pelvic ring. The
Young-Burgess classification system groups injuries according to the mechanism of
injury and severity of anatomic disruption. The Letournel classification describes the
anatomy of the fracture and joint disruptions observed with an injury pattern.
Tile classification
Tile type A: Injuries are rotationally and vertically stable and include avulsion injuries
that do not affect the pelvic ring, nondisplaced fractures of the pelvic ring, and
isolated transverse fractures of the sacrum.
Tile type B: Injuries with rotational instability of at least one hemipelvis, including
internal and external rotation patterns. The integrity of the posterior sacroiliac
ligaments and the posterior pelvic ring remain intact and prevent vertical instability.
Tile type C: Injuries with rotational and vertical instability of the hemipelvis(es).
Young-Burgess classification
Lateral compression (internal rotation) injuries
LC type I: Complete (bicortical) or incomplete (unicortical) fractures of the sacrum
with associated fractures (or dislocations) of the anterior pelvic ring (rami and/or
symphysis). A wide spectrum of injury and stability exists within these injuries.
LC type II: Complete fractures of the iliac wing that involve the sacroiliac joint to
varying degrees, leaving a crescent fragment of the ilium attached to the sacrum
via the posterior sacroiliac ligaments. Associated injuries to the sacrum and the
superior and inferior pubic ramus(i) also are present.
LC type III: An ipsilateral LC type I or LC type II injury associated with an external
rotation injury of the contralateral hemipelvis and complete or incomplete injuries
of the sacroiliac joint.
Anteroposterior compression (external rotation) injuries
APC type I: Isolated disruption of the symphyseal ligaments, with intact pelvic floor,
sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, and sacroiliac ligaments.
APC type II: Disruption of the symphyseal ligaments, anterior sacroiliac ligaments
with or without disruption of the sacrospinous and/or sacrotuberous ligaments,

Vertical shear injuries: Injuries associated with posterior and axial shear of a

Combined mechanism of injury: Pattern that may be severe and does not fit into

Traumatic lumbopelvic dissociation
Fractures described as U, Y or H pattern based on the morphology of the sacral
fracture and associated injuries to the anterior pelvic ring.14
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial evaluation of any trauma patient begins with a patient history and physical
examination.
The initial physical examination should follow ATLS protocol with assessment of the airway,
breathing, and circulation.

Patient History and Physical Examination

A thorough and detailed patient history and physical examination in the emergency
department is critical in the evaluation of all trauma patients. For patients in extremis or
those with signs of advanced shock, lifesaving resuscitative measures are initiated as the
patient history and head-to-toe physical examination proceeds. The patient history
should focus on understanding the mechanism of injury, level of energy of the trauma,
and any pertinent medical history and medications that may affect the patient’s
response to trauma and therapeutic maneuvers. Reports from first responders,
witnesses, and family members, if available, are critical.
The physical examination follows the principles of ATLS protocol with assessment of the
airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. Life- and limb-saving treatment
options are applied before moving to the next step in ATLS protocol; occasionally, —this
involves the use of advanced therapeutics, including surgery. Resumption of ATLS
protocol and performing a complete physical examination after the patient is stabilized
is critical to avoid missing other injuries. Patients should be completely disrobed, and a
physical examination of the rectum, perineum, and genitalia should be performed to
ensure occult genitourinary and open injuries are identified. A detailed neurologic
examination should be performed and documented if possible.
Some patients may present to the emergency department with a circumferential pelvic
compression device (pelvic binder or sheet) in place that was applied in the field or at a
transferring institution (Figure 10). This device should be left in place in patients in shock
with hemodynamic instability until hemodynamic stability is restored and/or adequate
skeletal stabilization is achieved.

Completion of perineal and genital physical examination is performed after the binder or
sheet is removed. Thorough inspection of the anus, rectum, perineal skin, labia, vaginal
wall, and urethral meatus in all patients with known or suspected pelvic fractures is
essential. Open wounds involving the anus, perineal skin, or labia are obvious red flags
for open pelvic fracture; however, lacerations of the rectal or vaginal wall are not readily
apparent and also may be associated with open fracture. Blood at the urethral meatus
indicates a potential bladder or urethral injury.
Imaging Studies
A screening AP pelvis radiograph on initiation of ATLS protocol allows for rapid diagnosis of
pelvic fractures and prevents delayed treatment (Figure 11).
A pelvic ring injury may be missed if imaging studies are obtained with a circumferential pelvic
compression device in place, which may reduce severe pelvic ring disruptions (Figure 12).

CT with 2-mm cuts through the entire pelvis helps define the injury, the degree of
displacement of fractures, associated dislocations, and pelvic bony anatomy for surgical
planning.
Soft tissue CT windows may help providers identify associated injuries, such as pelvic arterial
injury (Figure 13), outside of the musculoskeletal system.
Contrast-enhanced evaluation of the genitourinary tract (retrograde cystourethrography
(Figure 14) or CT cystourethrography) is a critical aspect of the evaluation of patients with a
displaced pelvic fracture.
MRI can be used to identify ligamentous injury in the pelvic ring or occult fractures, especially
in patients with osteopenia and unexplained pain; however, MRI findings have not been shown
to reliably correlate with stability or instability.

Imaging Studies
Some surgeons have suggested the screening AP pelvic radiograph be removed from
ATLS protocol; however, omission of the screening AP pelvic radiograph has been shown
to delay diagnosis by more than 45 minutes in some patients with major injuries (hip
dislocations) and results in increased radiation exposure secondary to the need for
repeat CT after reduction of hip dislocations.15 CT is necessary to fully define the
fractures and dislocations; displacement; and anatomic details, such as sacral
dysmorphism, which are critical to safe application of optimal surgical management.
Circumferential pelvic compression in place may mask injuries, including complete
sacroiliac joint dislocations, on imaging studies.16,17 Radiographs and CT scans are static
images of dynamic injuries, and examination under anesthesia with fluoroscopy may
help reveal the true extent of skeletal instability.18

Plain radiographs aid in identifying various injuries to the pelvic osseous and
ligamentous structures and the quality of reduction after therapeutic interventions. They
also are used for follow-up examinations to evaluate for loss of reduction and assess
healing. Although plain radiographs afford a good picture of overall pelvic ring
symmetry, CT scans are superior in evaluating the safe placement of fixation and the
quality of reduction, particularly at the level of the sacroiliac joint and the sacrum. AP,
inlet, and outlet radiographs of the pelvis should be obtained with the pubic symphysis
in-line with the spinous processes (rotational injuries notwithstanding). For an AP view,
the caudal aspect of the coccyx should be approximately 2 cm above the pubic
symphysis. An inlet view is oriented so the anterior aspect of the first and second sacral
segments overlap. An outlet view generally positions the pubic symphysis over the
second sacral segment but, ideally, is performed so the sacral foramina are visualized en
face. Evaluation of internal or external rotation and anterior and posterior translational
deformities is best performed on an inlet view. Cranial/caudal displacement,
flexion/extension, and the sacral foramina are best visualized on an outlet view. Pelvic
alignment and bony anatomy differ substantially between patients; however, inlet and
outlet radiographs obtained in 25° and 60° of caudal and cranial tilt, respectively,
generally provide sufficient information.19 CT scans can be used to determine the
precise tilt for inlet and outlet views20 and can be reconstructed into radiograph-like
images. A paradoxical inlet of the cranial sacral segments and an outlet view of the
caudal sacrum observed on an AP radiograph may indicate traumatic lumbopelvic
dissociation with a kyphotic deformity.
Computed Tomography
CT is considered the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of pelvic ring disruption.
(Figure 17)
The musculoskeletal structures and the surrounding soft tissues are evaluated and aid in
diagnosis and preoperative planning.

Computed Tomography
CT scans of the pelvis frequently are obtained during the routine workup of trauma
patients undergoing chest and abdominal scans. CT with 2-mm cuts through the pelvis
are obtained to fully evaluate the extent of musculoskeletal injury. With modern CT
software and technology, volume- and surface-rendered reconstruction images of the
bony pelvis can be used to create AP, inlet, and outlet views and three-dimensional
models that can be manipulated by the surgeon. Soft-tissue windows allow the physician
to assess for air in soft tissues outside of hollow organs that may indicate open injury.
Hematoma in the intrapelvic space and displacement of organs indicates bleeding and
internal degloving (Morel-Lavallee) lesions, which are visualized with hematoma in the
soft tissues about fascial planes (Figure 18). Chronic or acute hernias, lumbar and
inguinal resulting from injury can be identified and managed in combination with
musculoskeletal injuries. If arterial contrast is added to the imaging protocol, a blush
may signify active arterial bleeding (Figure 13); however, the low interobserver reliability
and low predictive ability associated with this technique make it controversial and
unreliable as a sole indicator of arterial hemorrhage indicating more advanced
interventions.21,22

MRI also is used to identify stress fractures of the pelvic ring not observed on plain
radiographs or CT scans (Figure 20).

Ligamentous structures are easily identified via MRI, and disruption in pelvic ring injuries
can be observed.23 The utility of MRI to direct management of pelvic ring disruptions is
uncertain; therefore, it is rarely used in patients with acute trauma. MRI findings do not
correlate with demonstrable instability of the pelvic ring. MRI is more useful for
evaluating occult insufficiency fractures, particularly sacral fractures in patients with
osteopenia and posterior pain if radiographs and CT scans do not demonstrate an
identifiable fracture.24
Management
Acute Management
Acute management largely depends on associated injuries and the hemodynamic status of the
patient.
The goal of management of a pelvic ring disruption is to restore and/or maintain appropriate
reduction of the pelvic ring until adequate bony and/or ligamentous healing has occurred.
The timing of acute and definitive management is dictated by other injuries and the
physiologic and hemodynamic status of the patient.
All patients should be evaluated using ATLS protocol, and resuscitation should begin
immediately for patients in shock. If indicated, blood product resuscitation with massive
transfusion protocols should be administered via a 1:1:1 ratio of packed red blood cells to
fresh frozen plasma to platelets.25
Hospital-based multidisciplinary protocols decrease mortality and create routines that
facilitate teamwork between the multiple subspecialties necessary to provide care for these
patients.26,27
Circumferential pelvic compression should be placed as early as possible in any patient with
hemodynamic instability and a volume-expanding pelvic ring injury. Liberal use in the field
and emergency departments for blunt trauma patients without known fracture or volume-
expanding injury is associated with little risk for harm and potentially limits ongoing blood
loss.
Appropriate placement of circumferential pelvic compression (binders or sheets) requires
multiple participants to pull traction, adduct, and internally rotate the lower extremities as
the pelvis is compressed from lateral to medial and the device is applied over the trochanters
(Figure 21, A). The device is not used to reduce the pelvis because this creates shear forces

Pelvic sheets or binders should not be removed until a patient is hemodynamically stable or
adequate stability of volume-expanding injuries of the pelvic ring has been attained with the
use of temporary or permanent internal or external fixation devices.
If abdominal or inguinal access is necessary for general surgery or interventional
radiography, a second binder or sheet may be placed more distally on the proximal thighs
before releasing the initial binder or sheet. Alternatively, holes may be cut in the binder or
sheet to provide appropriate access without losing the stabilization provided by
circumferential compression (Figure 21, B).
For injuries with vertical instability of a hemipelvis, 20 to 30 lbs of skeletal traction through
the distal femur or proximal tibia aids in provisional reduction and prevention of additional
deformity during the resuscitative phase (Figure 22). If longitudinal skeletal traction is placed
through the proximal tibia, ligamentous injury of the knee should be ruled out via a physical
examination before traction and via radiography after its application.

The orthopaedic surgeon should be in constant communication with the urologist during the
placement of suprapubic catheters that may interfere with subsequent surgical approaches
and definitive reconstruction.
Similar levels of communication are required with interventional radiologists with regard to
selective and nonselective methods for the management of pelvic hemorrhage because
these may interfere with subsequent reconstructive efforts.
External fixation and resuscitative iliosacral screws
Anterior pelvic external fixators should be placed under fluoroscopic guidance (Figures 21, B
and 23) and should not be used in isolation as definitive fixation in patients with complete
injuries of the posterior pelvic ring.
Resuscitative iliosacral screws are placed under fluoroscopic guidance in patients in shock
who have a completely unstable sacroiliac joint dislocation. Quality of reduction may be
sacrificed in the resuscitative phase, with subsequent revision performed after the patient is
more stable (Figure 24).

Acute Management
Circumferential pelvic compression with the use of sheets and binders has replaced
emergent external fixation in many centers because anterior external fixators
necessitate fluoroscopy for accurate and safe pin placement. Binders and sheets may be
placed in any environment, including a prehospital setting. Maintenance of provisional
stabilization of the pelvis with the use of a sheet or binder during external fixator
placement ensures the stability provided by circumferential pelvic compression is not
lost.
Anterior external fixation of the pelvic ring in patients with an incomplete injury of the
posterior pelvic ring is effective in reducing pelvic volume and providing stability to the
pelvis; however, in patients with a complete injury of the posterior pelvic ring, anterior
external fixation in isolation may accentuate the posterior deformity and, therefore, fail
to reduce pelvic volume (Figure 25). Maintenance of a sheet or binder in combination
with the use of an anterior external fixator may limit this displacement. In patients with a
complete injury of the posterior pelvic ring, the application of an anterior external fixator
should follow the same principles as circumferential pelvic compression placement;
lateral to medial directed pressure is applied over the trochanters to reduce the
deformity, after which the fixator is secured (do not use the fixator to reduce the
deformity).

Iliosacral screws can be placed percutaneously to compress the posterior pelvic ring and
reduce pelvic volume in patients with hemodynamic instability. Holes may be cut in
pelvic sheets and binders to allow for screw placement without loss of provisional
skeletal stability. This is particularly valuable in patients in whom circumferential pelvic
compression has reduced the deformity. In hemodynamically unstable patients, the
quality of reduction is less important than reducing pelvic volume and stabilizing the
pelvic ring to allow resuscitation to progress. Revision can be performed after the patient
has been fully resuscitated and is physiologically stable for more invasive surgical
procedures.
Advanced Resuscitation Measures
Many advanced resuscitation measures are used, and substantial controversy and
disagreement exists between practitioners with regard to the optimal modalities or
algorithms.
An institutional protocol that is followed by all practitioners for all patients is important.
These measures include pre-peritoneal pelvic packing with or without external fixation, pelvic
angiography with selective angioembolization, and retrograde endovascular balloon occlusion
of the aorta (Figure 26).

Advanced Resuscitation Measures
Indications for and the use of advanced resuscitation measures are controversial.
Institutional protocols with various treatment methods have improved mortality over
time. A protocol emphasizing appropriate volume resuscitation, circumferential pelvic
compression, and pelvic angiography within 60 minutes has been associated with a
mortality rate of 11% despite patients presenting with increased injury severity score.26
Lengthy delays to interventional radiography in certain centers have prompted general
and orthopaedic trauma surgeons to perform pre-peritoneal pelvic packing with or
without pelvic anterior external fixation as an alternative.28,29 A mortality rate of 21%
was reported in patients with a hemodynamically unstable pelvic ring injury and shock
refractory to transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells who underwent
emergent external fixation and pre-peritoneal pelvic packing compared with an overall
mortality rate of 8% in all patients presenting with a pelvic ring disruption at a level I
trauma center.27 Recently, retrograde endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta was
introduced as a minimally invasive method of temporarily occluding the aorta in patients
with advanced shock. Precise indications for use in patients with a hemodynamically
unstable pelvic ring disruption have not been established, and a nationwide analysis
comparing severely injured patients with and without retrograde endovascular balloon
occlusion of the aorta demonstrated higher mortality rates, acute kidney injury rates,
and lower leg amputation rates.30

Pearls and Pitfalls
20% to 25% of polytrauma patients will have a pelvic ring disruption.
Pelvic ring disruptions occur in a bimodal pattern with high-energy trauma occurring in
younger patients and low-energy mechanism of injury occurring in older patients with
osteopenia.
The screening AP pelvis radiograph obtained early in the ATLS protocol rapidly identifies
potentially life-threatening pelvic ring disruptions.
Patients with pelvic ring disruption and shock on arrival at the emergency department have
increased mortality.
CT of the pelvis with 2-mm cuts allow the surgical team to identify associated injuries, define
traumatic injury to the pelvic ring, and assess individual patient bony anatomy for safe implant
placement.
Circumferential pelvic compression should be placed as early as possible in patients with
volume-expanding pelvic ring injuries who have hypotension.
Pelvic sheets and binders should not be removed until a patient is hemodynamically stable
and musculoskeletal stability has been reestablished.
Pelvic sheets and binders may reduce and mask injuries to the pelvic ring, and radiography or
stress examinations out of circumferential compression should be performed after a patient is
hemodynamically stable.
Anterior external fixation best reduces pelvic volume in patients with an incomplete injury of
the posterior pelvic ring.
Hospital-based multidisciplinary protocols reduce mortality over time and require teamwork
between multiple specialties for success.
